structured.name: Liechtenstein
structured._source: wikidata (CC0); landBorders + naturalResources from CIA World Factbook (public domain)

prose.hook: Liechtenstein sits wedged between Austria and Switzerland, making it one of only two doubly landlocked countries in the world, alongside Uzbekistan. Its mountainous Alpine terrain hides an outsized economic punch: this tiny state exports specialty machinery, audio-video connectors, motor vehicle parts, dental products, and hardware, and draws on hydroelectric potential and arable land in its Rhine Valley.
prose.physicalGeography: Liechtenstein lies in Central Europe, sandwiched between Austria and Switzerland. The country is mostly mountainous, part of the Alps, with a strip of flatter Rhine Valley land running through its western third.
prose.climate: The climate is continental, with cold, cloudy winters bringing frequent snow or rain, and summers that are cool to moderately warm, cloudy, and humid. The mountainous terrain leaves the country exposed to avalanches and landslides.
prose.economy: Liechtenstein is a high-income European economy and a participant in the Schengen Area, functioning as a key European financial leader. It is closely integrated with the Swiss economy and uses the Swiss franc, and it ranks among the countries with the highest GDP per capita, though it depends on US and Eurozone markets to absorb its exports. Its industries include electronics, metal manufacturing, dental products, ceramics, pharmaceuticals, food products, precision instruments, optical instruments, and tourism, while its exports center on small specialty machinery, audio-video connectors, motor vehicle parts, dental products, and hardware.
prose.peopleAndCulture: Roman Catholicism is the official religion and the faith of about 73% of the population, with smaller communities of Protestant Reformed, Muslim, Christian Orthodox, Lutheran, and other Christian believers, alongside those with no religion or unspecified affiliation. Ethnically, Liechtensteiners make up roughly two-thirds of residents, with Swiss, Austrian, German, and Italian minorities accounting for most of the rest.
